Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- libnn-wiki-writer: Internal style guide for writing docs/wiki/ pages during /libnn-optimizer learn phase. Not a standalone skill -- read by the optimize agent.
- mlir-transform-writer: Write MLIR transform dialect scripts that directly control IR lowering - tiling, fusion, vectorization, bufferization, GPU thread mapping, shared memory promotion, and more. Use this skill whenever someone asks to generate, write, or modify a transform dialect script, transform library, codegen strategy, or tuning spec in MLIR. Also trigger when the request involves composing IR transformations for linalg ops, controlling IREE codegen pipelines via transform dialect, or replacing annotation-only configs with full transform strategies. Covers both upstream MLIR transform ops and IREE-specific extensions.
- spec-human: Create a human-reviewable architecture spec using a 6-section template (Summary, Background, Architecture, Interface, Edge Cases, Alternatives) BEFORE implementing a non-trivial design. Triggered explicitly via /spec-human <topic>, or when the user says "write a human spec", "create a review-ready design doc", "spec this out for review", or "I need a spec for X before we build it". Produces an ASCII markdown document at ./specs/<slug>.md aimed at peer engineers and tech leads who need to validate core architecture and trade-offs in 5 minutes. Do NOT auto-trigger on general design questions or coding tasks - this is a deliberate review gate that only fires on explicit request. For LLM-targeted specs (future sibling skill), use /spec-llm instead.
- iree-optimizer: Agentic per-dispatch tile-size tuner for IREE CPU codegen on RISC-V. Keeps IREE's chosen pipeline (CPUDoubleTilingExpert / CPUConvTileAndDecomposeExpert / CPUBufferOpsTileAndVectorize) and only overrides the root linalg op's lowering_config<tile_sizes = [...]>. Each round reads the best-so-far RISC-V assembly (LMUL, VLmax, register spills) to ground the next tile-size proposal; pre-compile divisibility gate ensures tiles divide their parent extents (no tail loop); a post-compile check of the IR after iree-codegen-generic-vectorization confirms no tail/masked main path. Compiles via iree_tuner.py, benchmarks on FPGA, iterates. Use whenever the user mentions tuning IREE dispatch tile sizes, agentic tile search, or wants to replace GA-based tile-size search with LLM-driven search. Trigger on "iree optimize", "optimize dispatch", "tile tune", or references to dispatch .mlir files for performance tuning.
- libnn-optimizer: Autonomous optimization workflow for libnn RISC-V neural network library functions
in the agentic_libnn_opt project. Use this skill when the user wants to optimize a
libnn function for FPGA performance, run the libnn optimization loop, validate the
optimization config, parse FPGA hardware features, extract shapes from perf test files,
or manage the optimization state machine. Trigger when: user mentions "optimize",
"libnn", "FPGA perf", "optimization loop", "validate config",
"phase gather/baseline/iterate/evaluate", "perf test", or references opt/config.toml,
opt/state.json, or any libnn function optimization task.

Use when the user wants to enable/disable behavior logging, analyze Claude Code session logs, list saved logs, or understand Claude Code's tool usage patterns. Trigger on: "cc-log", "behavior log", "system log", "record behavior", "log enable", "log disable", "analyze log".
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

1	# Switching-Mode Tutorial and Exercises
2	
3	Status: draft for review
4	Audience: engineer running the hybrid co-simulator for the first time
5	Scope: every switching mode (M1-M8) the repo ships, with copy-paste
6	commands and one exercise per mode.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0. What "switching mode" means
11	
12	The hybrid simulator runs a program across three phases:
13	
14	```
15	   QEMU1  --(state file + shared mmap)-->  vsim  --(state file + same mmap)-->  QEMU2
16	   (fast)                                 (cycle accurate)                       (fast)
17	```
18	
19	A "switching mode" is the RULE that decides WHEN each leg drains its
20	state and hands off. The codebase ships eight rules (M1-M8). They
21	plug into the same harness; you pick the rule with plugin args and
22	vsim CLI flags. The fixture binary does NOT need to change between
23	rules (one fixture can be driven by several modes).
24	
25	This document teaches one mode at a time, then exercises that
26	combine modes.
27	
28	### Quick map
29	
30	| ID | Name                           | Drain trigger                                   | Used at        |
31	|----|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------------|
32	| M1 | CSR insn match (default)       | `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` (enter) / `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` (exit) | QEMU1, vsim    |
33	| M2 | PC / ROI resolve               | PC equals an ROI boundary: any symbol or `0x` address (default `_hybrid_{enter,exit}_pc`) | QEMU1, vsim    |
34	| M3 | icount                         | N retired instructions                          | QEMU1, vsim    |
35	| M4 | BBV profile + SimPoint cluster | Plugin emits 1 row per slice; offline clustering | QEMU1 + tool   |
36	| M5 | slice-consume                  | End of slice index K                             | QEMU1          |
37	| M6 | archive emit                   | After drain, write `snap/K/{state.bin, mem, meta.json}` | orchestrator |
38	| M7 | checkpoint replay              | Hydrate `snap/K/` into a fresh mmap, resume      | orchestrator   |
39	| M8 | end-of-program                 | QEMU2 exits via semihosting `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED`  | QEMU2          |
40	
41	M1/M2/M3 are entry/exit triggers (the "boundary" question).
42	M4/M5/M6/M7 are pipeline stages for the full SimPoint flow.
43	M8 is the natural end-of-run signal (always at the tail).
44	
45	---
46	
47	## 1. One-time prerequisites
48	
49	Build everything once. Each command is idempotent.
50	
51	```sh
52	cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
53	source ./setup.sh         # qemu + vsim + plugin + simpoint
54	```
55	
56	You should now have:
57	
58	| Artifact                                  | Purpose                           |
59	|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
60	| `build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64`          | QEMU binary (phase 1 and phase 3) |
61	| `verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium`   | vsim binary (phase 2)             |
62	| `qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so`        | TCG plugin (state drainer)        |
63	| `tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint`             | SimPoint clustering tool (M4)     |
64	| `tests/fixtures/*.elf`           | Test fixtures (e.g. rt_c_v_regs)  |
65	
66	Common env vars (auto-detected by every demo; override only if you
67	keep these elsewhere):
68	
69	```sh
70	export VSIM_QEMU=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64
71	export VSIM_PLUGIN=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so
72	export VSIM_BIN=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium
73	```
74	
75	---
76	
77	## 2. M1 + M8 - CSR insn match (the default path)
78	
79	### What it does
80	
81	QEMU1's plugin pattern-matches the encoding `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` at retire
82	time. On hit it drains state to `outfile` and exits 200. vsim does the
83	same on `csrwi 0x7C0, 1`. CSR 0x7C0 is a benign vendor write on Andes
84	ax45mp, so the fixture binary embeds these two `csrwi` instructions
85	at the ROI boundaries.
86	
87	M8 is automatic: after vsim hands back, QEMU2 finishes the workload
88	and exits via `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED` semihosting.
89	
90	### Inputs
91	
92	- Fixture ELF with `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` and `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` in its source.
93	  Every C-level fixture (rt_c_v_regs, rt_c_matmul, etc.) has these.
94	
95	### Output
96	
97	- Phase-by-phase log line + final `exit 0`.
98	
99	### Run it
100	
101	```sh
102	cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
103	bash tests/demos/demo_csr_oneshot.sh
104	```
105	
106	Expected last line:
107	
108	```
109	[demo M1] PASS (CSR insn match (M1+M8))
110	```
111	
112	### Drill-down (what the demo does internally)
113	
114	Inside, the demo calls the generic harness:
115	
116	```sh
117	FIXTURE=rt_c_v_regs TRIGGER_MODE=csr EXPECT_RC=0 \
118	  bash tests/e2e.sh
119	```
120	
121	The plugin gets `outfile=<state.bin>` and nothing else - that is the
122	M1 default. vsim is launched without `--hybrid-exit-pc` and without
123	`--hybrid-icount`, so its ELF pre-scanner watches for `csrwi 0x7C0, 1`
124	PCs at retire.
125	
126	### Exercise 1
127	
128	Switch fixture from `rt_c_v_regs` to `rt_c_matmul`. The script is
129	fixture-parameterized:
130	
131	```sh
132	FIXTURE=rt_c_matmul TRIGGER_MODE=csr EXPECT_RC=0 \
133	  bash tests/e2e.sh
134	```
135	
136	Verify the last line says `PASS: round-trip exit code 0`. Then read
137	`tests/fixtures/rt_c_matmul.c` and confirm where the two
138	`csrwi 0x7C0, *` markers live (`enter_vsim()` / `exit_vsim()` helpers).
139	
140	---
141	
142	## 3. M2 - PC symbol resolve
143	
144	### What it does
145	
146	Same round-trip as M1 but the trigger is a PC value (not an opcode
147	match). The harness resolves each ROI boundary - taken from
148	`ROI_START` / `ROI_END`, which default to the symbols `_hybrid_enter_pc`
149	and `_hybrid_exit_pc` - to an address (a `0x` value is used verbatim; a
150	name is looked up with `nm`), then passes:
151	
152	- `enter_pc=0x<addr>` to the QEMU plugin (QEMU1 drains there)
153	- `--hybrid-exit-pc 0x<addr>` to vsim (vsim drains there)
154	
155	CSR-mode matchers are bypassed; the `csrwi 0x7C0, *` instructions in
156	the binary become inert (CSR 0x7C0 is a benign vendor-defined write).
157	
158	This proves you can hand off WITHOUT modifying the source: point the ROI
159	at any function or address the binary already has.
160	
161	### Inputs
162	
163	- Same fixture as M1 (`rt_c_v_regs`). With the defaults, the ELF must
164	  define `_hybrid_enter_pc` / `_hybrid_exit_pc` (the C-level fixtures all
165	  do). To target a different region, set `ROI_START` / `ROI_END` (or
166	  `./hsim run --roi-start/--roi-end`) to any symbol or `0x` address - then
167	  no marker symbols are needed at all.
168	
169	### Output
170	
171	- `exit 0`, last log line `[demo M2] PASS`.
172	
173	### Run it
174	
175	```sh
176	bash tests/demos/demo_pc_oneshot.sh
177	```
178	
179	### Drill-down
180	
181	```sh
182	ENTER_PC=$(riscv64-unknown-elf-nm --defined-only \
183	              tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf | \
184	              awk '$3=="_hybrid_enter_pc"{print $1}')
185	EXIT_PC=$(riscv64-unknown-elf-nm --defined-only \
186	              tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf | \
187	              awk '$3=="_hybrid_exit_pc"{print $1}')
188	
189	# QEMU plugin arg
190	... -plugin libhybrid_handoff.so,outfile=$STATE,enter_pc=0x$ENTER_PC
191	
192	# vsim arg
193	... --hybrid-exit-pc 0x$EXIT_PC
194	```
195	
196	### Exercise 2
197	
198	Compare exit values: run the demo with TRIGGER_MODE=csr and again
199	with TRIGGER_MODE=pc on the same fixture. Both must exit 0 and
200	both must drain the same PC. Use:
201	
202	```sh
203	xxd state_csr.bin | head -4
204	xxd state_pc.bin  | head -4
205	```
206	
207	The PC field is at offset 16 (`hybrid_state_v1::pc`). For most
208	fixtures `pc(csr) == pc(pc)` because both modes drain right after
209	the entry trigger retires.
210	
211	---
212	
213	## 4. M3 - icount round-trip
214	
215	### What it does
216	
217	Both legs drain on retired-instruction count alone. No CSR, no PC
218	symbol. Suitable for CSR-less workloads (an infinite spin loop, a
219	benchmark you cannot edit, etc.).
220	
221	- QEMU plugin: `icount=N1` -> drain at the N1-th retired insn
222	- vsim: `--hybrid-icount N2` -> drain N2 insns after resume
223	
224	### Inputs
225	
226	- Any ELF; `icount_spin.elf` is the canonical CSR-less fixture.
227	
228	### Output
229	
230	- Both QEMU1 and vsim exit 200 with a non-empty state file. There is
231	  no QEMU2 phase because `icount_spin` spins forever (no natural
232	  semihosting exit).
233	
234	### Run it
235	
236	```sh
237	bash tests/demos/demo_icount_roundtrip.sh
238	```
239	
240	Override targets:
241	
242	```sh
243	QEMU_ICOUNT=20000 VSIM_ICOUNT=8000 \
244	  bash tests/demos/demo_icount_roundtrip.sh
245	```
246	
247	### Exercise 3
248	
249	Predict where the drained PC will land for `icount_spin.elf`. The
250	loop body has two RVC instructions at PCs `0x100002` and `0x100004`.
251	Run with VSIM_ICOUNT=5000. The drained PC should be one of those
252	two values. Read the demo's `read_u64` helper to confirm how the PC
253	is extracted from the state file (offset 16, little-endian 8 bytes).
254	
255	---
256	
257	## 5. M4 - BBV profile + SimPoint cluster
258	
259	### What it does
260	
261	QEMU plugin emits one Basic-Block-Vector (BBV) row per slice of N
262	retired insns. The output is a SimPoint `.bb` file. Offline,
263	`tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint` reads it and clusters the rows into K
264	representative phases.
265	
266	This is the SimPoint "profile" pass. It produces:
267	
268	- `simpts` file: 1 line per cluster, `<slice_idx> <cluster_id>`
269	- `weights` file: 1 line per cluster, `<weight> <cluster_id>`
270	
271	Later, M5+M6+M7 replay just those representative slices.
272	
273	### Inputs
274	
275	- Any ELF. CSR-less or not - the plugin emits BBV rows regardless.
276	
277	### Output
278	
279	- `WORKDIR/<elf>.bb`, `WORKDIR/simpts`, `WORKDIR/weights` persist on
280	  disk so that M5/M7 can consume them.
281	
282	### Run it
283	
284	```sh
285	WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-profile \
286	  bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
287	```
288	
289	Override the slice and total count:
290	
291	```sh
292	WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-bigger SLICE=2000 ICOUNT=20000 MAXK=4 \
293	  bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
294	```
295	
296	Expected rows = `ICOUNT / SLICE`. The demo asserts this.
297	
298	### Drill-down: plugin args
299	
300	```
301	-plugin libhybrid_handoff.so,\
302	        outfile=$STATE,\
303	        bbv_out=$WORKDIR/profile.bb,\
304	        slice=1000,\
305	        icount=10000
306	```
307	
308	`slice` is shared with M5; `bbv_out=` is what activates emit mode.
309	
310	### Exercise 4
311	
312	Run the demo with WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-ex SLICE=500 ICOUNT=10000 MAXK=3.
313	Inspect `simpts` and `weights`. The number of lines in each file
314	must be equal and at most `MAXK`. Sum the first column of `weights`
315	- it should be approximately 1.0 (SimPoint may emit unnormalised on
316	small inputs; the demo prints this sum for sanity-check).
317	
318	---
319	
320	## 6. M5 - slice-consume entry
321	
322	### What it does
323	
324	QEMU plugin drains at the end of slice K (0-based), where each slice
325	is N retired insns. This is the SimPoint "replay" entry: you ran M4
326	once, picked phase K, and now you want vsim to start from the END of
327	slice K (the QEMU drain leaves you with exactly that architectural
328	state).
329	
330	Plugin args:
331	
332	- `slice=N` (insns per slice; SAME N as the profile pass)
333	- `slice_at=K` (drain at the end of the K-th slice, 0-based)
334	- `icount=M` (safety fallback - if K is invalid, drain at M anyway)
335	
336	### Inputs
337	
338	- Same ELF as the profile pass. Same `slice=N`.
339	- K from `simpts` (T4 output) OR from env `SLICE_AT`.
340	
341	### Output
342	
343	- State file drained at the slice boundary. PC inside the ROI.
344	
345	### Run it
346	
347	Using M4's output directly:
348	
349	```sh
350	WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-profile bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
351	SIMPTS=/tmp/m4-profile/simpts \
352	  bash tests/demos/demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh
353	```
354	
355	Manual K choice:
356	
357	```sh
358	SLICE=1000 SLICE_AT=3 \
359	  bash tests/demos/demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh
360	```
361	
362	Inside, the demo combines two modes: M5 for entry (QEMU side) and
363	M3 for exit (vsim side, `--hybrid-icount`). They are independent;
364	each side picks its own mode.
365	
366	### Exercise 5
367	
368	Pipeline M4 -> M5 by hand (no demo script):
369	
370	1. Run M4 with `SLICE=1000 ICOUNT=10000 MAXK=2`. Note `WORKDIR`.
371	2. `cat $WORKDIR/simpts` and pick the first cluster's slice index, K.
372	3. Run vsim manually:
373	   - QEMU plugin `slice=1000,slice_at=K,outfile=...`
374	   - vsim `--resume-from-qemu STATE --hybrid-icount 5000 --handoff-out STATE_V`
375	4. Confirm both legs exit 200.
376	
377	This is exactly what `demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh` automates.
378	
379	---
380	
381	## 7. M6 + M7 - archive emit and checkpoint replay
382	
383	### What it does
384	
385	M6 packages a drained state plus its shared mmap into a portable
386	archive directory:
387	
388	```
389	snap/K/
390	  state.bin    # hybrid_state_v1 (8.5 KB)
391	  mem          # full shared mmap (128 MB by default)
392	  meta.json    # schema=1, abi_version=1, mmap_size, slice_index, etc.
393	```
394	
395	M7 replays an archive: hydrate `mem` into a fresh `/dev/shm` file,
396	hand `state.bin` to vsim (or QEMU), let it run to natural exit.
397	
398	Together they decouple "where the simulation ran" from "where the
399	simulation is replayed" - you can email an archive to a colleague.
400	
401	### Inputs
402	
403	- For M6: a plan YAML pointing at a fixture and a drain trigger.
404	- For M7: an existing archive directory and a target model
405	  (`--resume-with vsim` or `--resume-with qemu`).
406	
407	### Output
408	
409	- M6: `$ARCHIVE_ROOT/snap/0/{state.bin, mem, meta.json}`
410	- M7: replay exits 0 (or 200 if the replay also drains); PC advances
411	  past the archive's PC.
412	
413	### Run it
414	
415	```sh
416	WORKDIR=/tmp/m6m7 \
417	  bash tests/demos/demo_archive_replay.sh
418	```
419	
420	Switch the replay target to QEMU:
421	
422	```sh
423	RESUME_WITH=qemu WORKDIR=/tmp/m6m7-qemu \
424	  bash tests/demos/demo_archive_replay.sh
425	```
426	
427	### Drill-down: the plan YAML
428	
429	```yaml
430	session:
431	  mem_size: 134217728
432	  mmap_path: null
433	  elf: tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf
434	
435	steps:
436	  - model: qemu
437	    trigger: { kind: csr }
438	    on_exit: { archive_as: "snap/0" }
439	```
440	
441	The orchestrator parses this, spawns QEMU+plugin with `outfile=`,
442	waits for the drain (exit 200), then writes the archive.
443	
444	### Exercise 6
445	
446	Use M6 to capture two archives from the same workload at different
447	slice points, then M7 to replay both. Skeleton:
448	
449	1. Run T4 (M4) to get simpts.
450	2. For each `K` in simpts:
451	   - QEMU+plugin `slice=N,slice_at=K`, capture state.bin.
452	   - Python: `orchestrator.checkpoint.write_archive(...)` -> snap/K/
453	3. For each `snap/K/`:
454	   - `python3 -m orchestrator.main replay-checkpoint <snap/K>
455	       --resume-with vsim`
456	
457	This is exactly what T7 (`demo_simpoint_loop.sh`) automates.
458	
459	---
460	
461	## 8. Putting it all together: T7 (the centerpiece)
462	
463	`demo_simpoint_loop.sh` chains M4 -> M5 -> M6 -> M7 on
464	`rt_c_v_regs.elf`:
465	
466	```
467	M4  profile pass    : QEMU+plugin bbv_out=,slice=20,icount=2000
468	                      -> 15 BBV rows
469	---  cluster        : simpoint -maxK 2 -dim 2
470	                      -> 2 representative slice indices
471	M5  per phase       : QEMU+plugin slice=20,slice_at=K
472	                      -> state.bin drained at slice K
473	M6  per phase       : orchestrator.checkpoint.write_archive(...)
474	                      -> snap/K/{state.bin, mem, meta.json}
475	M7  per archive     : orchestrator.main replay-checkpoint --resume-with vsim
476	                      -> vsim resumes, drains naturally on csrwi 0x7C0,1 (M1+M8)
477	```
478	
479	Run it:
480	
481	```sh
482	WORKDIR=/tmp/t7 bash tests/demos/demo_simpoint_loop.sh
483	```
484	
485	Expected last line:
486	
487	```
488	[demo T7] PASS (Full SimPoint loop (M4 -> M5 -> M6 -> M7)): \
489	   bbv_rows=15 phases=2 replays_ok=2 workdir=/tmp/t7
490	```

# Switching-Mode Tutorial and Exercises

Status: draft for review
Audience: engineer running the hybrid co-simulator for the first time
Scope: every switching mode (M1-M8) the repo ships, with copy-paste
commands and one exercise per mode.

---

## 0. What "switching mode" means

The hybrid simulator runs a program across three phases:

```
   QEMU1  --(state file + shared mmap)-->  vsim  --(state file + same mmap)-->  QEMU2
   (fast)                                 (cycle accurate)                       (fast)
```

A "switching mode" is the RULE that decides WHEN each leg drains its
state and hands off. The codebase ships eight rules (M1-M8). They
plug into the same harness; you pick the rule with plugin args and
vsim CLI flags. The fixture binary does NOT need to change between
rules (one fixture can be driven by several modes).

This document teaches one mode at a time, then exercises that
combine modes.

### Quick map

| ID | Name                           | Drain trigger                                   | Used at        |
|----|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| M1 | CSR insn match (default)       | `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` (enter) / `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` (exit) | QEMU1, vsim    |
| M2 | PC / ROI resolve               | PC equals an ROI boundary: any symbol or `0x` address (default `_hybrid_{enter,exit}_pc`) | QEMU1, vsim    |
| M3 | icount                         | N retired instructions                          | QEMU1, vsim    |
| M4 | BBV profile + SimPoint cluster | Plugin emits 1 row per slice; offline clustering | QEMU1 + tool   |
| M5 | slice-consume                  | End of slice index K                             | QEMU1          |
| M6 | archive emit                   | After drain, write `snap/K/{state.bin, mem, meta.json}` | orchestrator |
| M7 | checkpoint replay              | Hydrate `snap/K/` into a fresh mmap, resume      | orchestrator   |
| M8 | end-of-program                 | QEMU2 exits via semihosting `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED`  | QEMU2          |

M1/M2/M3 are entry/exit triggers (the "boundary" question).
M4/M5/M6/M7 are pipeline stages for the full SimPoint flow.
M8 is the natural end-of-run signal (always at the tail).

---

## 1. One-time prerequisites

Build everything once. Each command is idempotent.

```sh
cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
source ./setup.sh         # qemu + vsim + plugin + simpoint
```

You should now have:

| Artifact                                  | Purpose                           |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64`          | QEMU binary (phase 1 and phase 3) |
| `verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium`   | vsim binary (phase 2)             |
| `qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so`        | TCG plugin (state drainer)        |
| `tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint`             | SimPoint clustering tool (M4)     |
| `tests/fixtures/*.elf`           | Test fixtures (e.g. rt_c_v_regs)  |

Common env vars (auto-detected by every demo; override only if you
keep these elsewhere):

```sh
export VSIM_QEMU=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64
export VSIM_PLUGIN=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so
export VSIM_BIN=/home/nick/work/hybrid_sim/verilator/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium
```

---

## 2. M1 + M8 - CSR insn match (the default path)

### What it does

QEMU1's plugin pattern-matches the encoding `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` at retire
time. On hit it drains state to `outfile` and exits 200. vsim does the
same on `csrwi 0x7C0, 1`. CSR 0x7C0 is a benign vendor write on Andes
ax45mp, so the fixture binary embeds these two `csrwi` instructions
at the ROI boundaries.

M8 is automatic: after vsim hands back, QEMU2 finishes the workload
and exits via `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED` semihosting.

### Inputs

- Fixture ELF with `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` and `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` in its source.
  Every C-level fixture (rt_c_v_regs, rt_c_matmul, etc.) has these.

### Output

- Phase-by-phase log line + final `exit 0`.

### Run it

```sh
cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
bash tests/demos/demo_csr_oneshot.sh
```

Expected last line:

```
[demo M1] PASS (CSR insn match (M1+M8))
```

### Drill-down (what the demo does internally)

Inside, the demo calls the generic harness:

```sh
FIXTURE=rt_c_v_regs TRIGGER_MODE=csr EXPECT_RC=0 \
  bash tests/e2e.sh
```

The plugin gets `outfile=<state.bin>` and nothing else - that is the
M1 default. vsim is launched without `--hybrid-exit-pc` and without
`--hybrid-icount`, so its ELF pre-scanner watches for `csrwi 0x7C0, 1`
PCs at retire.

### Exercise 1

Switch fixture from `rt_c_v_regs` to `rt_c_matmul`. The script is
fixture-parameterized:

```sh
FIXTURE=rt_c_matmul TRIGGER_MODE=csr EXPECT_RC=0 \
  bash tests/e2e.sh
```

Verify the last line says `PASS: round-trip exit code 0`. Then read
`tests/fixtures/rt_c_matmul.c` and confirm where the two
`csrwi 0x7C0, *` markers live (`enter_vsim()` / `exit_vsim()` helpers).

---

## 3. M2 - PC symbol resolve

### What it does

Same round-trip as M1 but the trigger is a PC value (not an opcode
match). The harness resolves each ROI boundary - taken from
`ROI_START` / `ROI_END`, which default to the symbols `_hybrid_enter_pc`
and `_hybrid_exit_pc` - to an address (a `0x` value is used verbatim; a
name is looked up with `nm`), then passes:

- `enter_pc=0x<addr>` to the QEMU plugin (QEMU1 drains there)
- `--hybrid-exit-pc 0x<addr>` to vsim (vsim drains there)

CSR-mode matchers are bypassed; the `csrwi 0x7C0, *` instructions in
the binary become inert (CSR 0x7C0 is a benign vendor-defined write).

This proves you can hand off WITHOUT modifying the source: point the ROI
at any function or address the binary already has.

### Inputs

- Same fixture as M1 (`rt_c_v_regs`). With the defaults, the ELF must
  define `_hybrid_enter_pc` / `_hybrid_exit_pc` (the C-level fixtures all
  do). To target a different region, set `ROI_START` / `ROI_END` (or
  `./hsim run --roi-start/--roi-end`) to any symbol or `0x` address - then
  no marker symbols are needed at all.

### Output

- `exit 0`, last log line `[demo M2] PASS`.

### Run it

```sh
bash tests/demos/demo_pc_oneshot.sh
```

### Drill-down

```sh
ENTER_PC=$(riscv64-unknown-elf-nm --defined-only \
              tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf | \
              awk '$3=="_hybrid_enter_pc"{print $1}')
EXIT_PC=$(riscv64-unknown-elf-nm --defined-only \
              tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf | \
              awk '$3=="_hybrid_exit_pc"{print $1}')

# QEMU plugin arg
... -plugin libhybrid_handoff.so,outfile=$STATE,enter_pc=0x$ENTER_PC

# vsim arg
... --hybrid-exit-pc 0x$EXIT_PC
```

### Exercise 2

Compare exit values: run the demo with TRIGGER_MODE=csr and again
with TRIGGER_MODE=pc on the same fixture. Both must exit 0 and
both must drain the same PC. Use:

```sh
xxd state_csr.bin | head -4
xxd state_pc.bin  | head -4
```

The PC field is at offset 16 (`hybrid_state_v1::pc`). For most
fixtures `pc(csr) == pc(pc)` because both modes drain right after
the entry trigger retires.

---

## 4. M3 - icount round-trip

### What it does

Both legs drain on retired-instruction count alone. No CSR, no PC
symbol. Suitable for CSR-less workloads (an infinite spin loop, a
benchmark you cannot edit, etc.).

- QEMU plugin: `icount=N1` -> drain at the N1-th retired insn
- vsim: `--hybrid-icount N2` -> drain N2 insns after resume

### Inputs

- Any ELF; `icount_spin.elf` is the canonical CSR-less fixture.

### Output

- Both QEMU1 and vsim exit 200 with a non-empty state file. There is
  no QEMU2 phase because `icount_spin` spins forever (no natural
  semihosting exit).

### Run it

```sh
bash tests/demos/demo_icount_roundtrip.sh
```

Override targets:

```sh
QEMU_ICOUNT=20000 VSIM_ICOUNT=8000 \
  bash tests/demos/demo_icount_roundtrip.sh
```

### Exercise 3

Predict where the drained PC will land for `icount_spin.elf`. The
loop body has two RVC instructions at PCs `0x100002` and `0x100004`.
Run with VSIM_ICOUNT=5000. The drained PC should be one of those
two values. Read the demo's `read_u64` helper to confirm how the PC
is extracted from the state file (offset 16, little-endian 8 bytes).

---

## 5. M4 - BBV profile + SimPoint cluster

### What it does

QEMU plugin emits one Basic-Block-Vector (BBV) row per slice of N
retired insns. The output is a SimPoint `.bb` file. Offline,
`tools/simpoint/bin/simpoint` reads it and clusters the rows into K
representative phases.

This is the SimPoint "profile" pass. It produces:

- `simpts` file: 1 line per cluster, `<slice_idx> <cluster_id>`
- `weights` file: 1 line per cluster, `<weight> <cluster_id>`

Later, M5+M6+M7 replay just those representative slices.

### Inputs

- Any ELF. CSR-less or not - the plugin emits BBV rows regardless.

### Output

- `WORKDIR/<elf>.bb`, `WORKDIR/simpts`, `WORKDIR/weights` persist on
  disk so that M5/M7 can consume them.

### Run it

```sh
WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-profile \
  bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
```

Override the slice and total count:

```sh
WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-bigger SLICE=2000 ICOUNT=20000 MAXK=4 \
  bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
```

Expected rows = `ICOUNT / SLICE`. The demo asserts this.

### Drill-down: plugin args

```
-plugin libhybrid_handoff.so,\
        outfile=$STATE,\
        bbv_out=$WORKDIR/profile.bb,\
        slice=1000,\
        icount=10000
```

`slice` is shared with M5; `bbv_out=` is what activates emit mode.

### Exercise 4

Run the demo with WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-ex SLICE=500 ICOUNT=10000 MAXK=3.
Inspect `simpts` and `weights`. The number of lines in each file
must be equal and at most `MAXK`. Sum the first column of `weights`
- it should be approximately 1.0 (SimPoint may emit unnormalised on
small inputs; the demo prints this sum for sanity-check).

---

## 6. M5 - slice-consume entry

### What it does

QEMU plugin drains at the end of slice K (0-based), where each slice
is N retired insns. This is the SimPoint "replay" entry: you ran M4
once, picked phase K, and now you want vsim to start from the END of
slice K (the QEMU drain leaves you with exactly that architectural
state).

Plugin args:

- `slice=N` (insns per slice; SAME N as the profile pass)
- `slice_at=K` (drain at the end of the K-th slice, 0-based)
- `icount=M` (safety fallback - if K is invalid, drain at M anyway)

### Inputs

- Same ELF as the profile pass. Same `slice=N`.
- K from `simpts` (T4 output) OR from env `SLICE_AT`.

### Output

- State file drained at the slice boundary. PC inside the ROI.

### Run it

Using M4's output directly:

```sh
WORKDIR=/tmp/m4-profile bash tests/demos/demo_bbv_profile.sh
SIMPTS=/tmp/m4-profile/simpts \
  bash tests/demos/demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh
```

Manual K choice:

```sh
SLICE=1000 SLICE_AT=3 \
  bash tests/demos/demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh
```

Inside, the demo combines two modes: M5 for entry (QEMU side) and
M3 for exit (vsim side, `--hybrid-icount`). They are independent;
each side picks its own mode.

### Exercise 5

Pipeline M4 -> M5 by hand (no demo script):

1. Run M4 with `SLICE=1000 ICOUNT=10000 MAXK=2`. Note `WORKDIR`.
2. `cat $WORKDIR/simpts` and pick the first cluster's slice index, K.
3. Run vsim manually:
   - QEMU plugin `slice=1000,slice_at=K,outfile=...`
   - vsim `--resume-from-qemu STATE --hybrid-icount 5000 --handoff-out STATE_V`
4. Confirm both legs exit 200.

This is exactly what `demo_slice_consume_roundtrip.sh` automates.

---

## 7. M6 + M7 - archive emit and checkpoint replay

### What it does

M6 packages a drained state plus its shared mmap into a portable
archive directory:

```
snap/K/
  state.bin    # hybrid_state_v1 (8.5 KB)
  mem          # full shared mmap (128 MB by default)
  meta.json    # schema=1, abi_version=1, mmap_size, slice_index, etc.
```

M7 replays an archive: hydrate `mem` into a fresh `/dev/shm` file,
hand `state.bin` to vsim (or QEMU), let it run to natural exit.

Together they decouple "where the simulation ran" from "where the
simulation is replayed" - you can email an archive to a colleague.

### Inputs

- For M6: a plan YAML pointing at a fixture and a drain trigger.
- For M7: an existing archive directory and a target model
  (`--resume-with vsim` or `--resume-with qemu`).

### Output

- M6: `$ARCHIVE_ROOT/snap/0/{state.bin, mem, meta.json}`
- M7: replay exits 0 (or 200 if the replay also drains); PC advances
  past the archive's PC.

### Run it

```sh
WORKDIR=/tmp/m6m7 \
  bash tests/demos/demo_archive_replay.sh
```

Switch the replay target to QEMU:

```sh
RESUME_WITH=qemu WORKDIR=/tmp/m6m7-qemu \
  bash tests/demos/demo_archive_replay.sh
```

### Drill-down: the plan YAML

```yaml
session:
  mem_size: 134217728
  mmap_path: null
  elf: tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_regs.elf

steps:
  - model: qemu
    trigger: { kind: csr }
    on_exit: { archive_as: "snap/0" }
```

The orchestrator parses this, spawns QEMU+plugin with `outfile=`,
waits for the drain (exit 200), then writes the archive.

### Exercise 6

Use M6 to capture two archives from the same workload at different
slice points, then M7 to replay both. Skeleton:

1. Run T4 (M4) to get simpts.
2. For each `K` in simpts:
   - QEMU+plugin `slice=N,slice_at=K`, capture state.bin.
   - Python: `orchestrator.checkpoint.write_archive(...)` -> snap/K/
3. For each `snap/K/`:
   - `python3 -m orchestrator.main replay-checkpoint <snap/K>
       --resume-with vsim`

This is exactly what T7 (`demo_simpoint_loop.sh`) automates.

---

## 8. Putting it all together: T7 (the centerpiece)

`demo_simpoint_loop.sh` chains M4 -> M5 -> M6 -> M7 on
`rt_c_v_regs.elf`:

```
M4  profile pass    : QEMU+plugin bbv_out=,slice=20,icount=2000

M7  per archive     : orchestrator.main replay-checkpoint --resume-with vsim

## 10. Switching-mode decision flow

When you have a new workload, pick a mode like this:

```

  yes -> Add csrwi 0x7C0, 0 and csrwi 0x7C0, 1 around the ROI -> M1
  no  -> Continue.

Is there a symbol or PC address at each ROI boundary?

         _hybrid_{enter,exit}_pc markers when present).
  no  -> Continue.

Do you know an instruction count where the ROI is hot?
  yes -> Use M3.
  no  -> Continue.

You want SimPoint phase-aware replay -> M4 + M5 + M6 + M7 (T7).
```

| `vsim drained pc=0x... not in icount_spin loop`         | VSIM_ICOUNT too small / wrong fixture                               |
| Whole suite times out under scripts/run_e2e.sh                  | `JOBS` too high; set `JOBS=8`                                       |

| M1 | CSR insn match (default) | `csrwi 0x7C0, 0` (enter) / `csrwi 0x7C0, 1` (exit) | QEMU1, vsim |

Grouping:
- **M1/M2/M3** - entry/exit boundary triggers (the "when to hand off" rule).
- **M4/M5/M6/M7** - pipeline stages of the full SimPoint flow.
- **M8** - natural end-of-run signal (always at the tail).

The `./hsim run` driver exposes four of these directly: `--mode csr` (M1), `pc` (M2), `icount` (M3), `slice` (M5).

A **slice** is a fixed window of N retired instructions. It is the unit SimPoint uses to chop a program's execution into equal chunks.

How it is used across the modes:

- **Counting unit**: slice index K means "the K-th block of N instructions" (0-based). Slice 0 = insns 0..N-1, slice 1 = insns N..2N-1, etc. The plugin arg `slice=N` sets the window size.

- **M4 (BBV profile)**: the plugin emits one Basic-Block-Vector row per slice. If you run 10000 insns with `slice=1000`, you get 10 rows. SimPoint clusters these rows to find which slices are "representative" phases of the program.

- **M5 (slice-consume)**: `slice=N,slice_at=K` tells QEMU1 to drain exactly at the end of slice K. This is the replay entry: after M4 told you slice K is a hot/representative phase, you fast-forward QEMU to the end of slice K, then hand that architectural state to vsim.

Why it matters: real workloads run billions of instructions. You cannot cycle-accurately simulate all of them. SimPoint says "these few slices represent the whole program," so you only run vsim on those slices and extrapolate. The slice is the granularity of that sampling.

In `./hsim run --mode slice`, you pick the slice size and which slice to stop at, instead of relying on a CSR/PC marker in the binary.

The root problem: "M1-M8" is not one list. It is three different questions stacked into one numbering:

- **When to drain** (the trigger): M1 csr, M2 pc, M3 icount, M5 slice
- **What to do after a drain** (persistence): M6 emit, M7 replay
- **How the run ends** (tail): M8

Per mode:

- **M1** answers *when does QEMU1 hand off?* It is the default trigger, a peer of pc/icount/slice. Different question from the others.
- **M6 + M7** are one feature with two verbs: emit writes `snap/K/`, replay reads it back. The archive format is the contract between them. This merge is correct - call it one `checkpoint` concept (emit / replay).
- **M8** is not a selectable mode at all. Every workload that finishes ends at QEMU2's semihosting exit. There is nothing to "merge with" - it is the default tail of M1, M6, M7, and everything else. Demote it, do not group it.

| Axis | Pick one / optional | Replaces |
|------|---------------------|----------|
| Trigger (when to drain) | csr / pc / icount / slice | M1, M2, M3, M5 |
| Profile (optional sidecar) | BBV + SimPoint | M4 |
| Checkpoint (optional) | emit + replay | **M6 + M7** |
| Tail (always on, not a mode) | QEMU2 semihosting exit | M8 -> dropped |

2	
3	> Notes archive | Author: Nick Hung | Date: 2026-05-22
4	> Companion to gem5-cpu-model-switch.md (trigger source 3.6).
5	
6	## TL;DR
7	
8	There is no fixed warmup instruction count. Both modes run a `TimingSimpleCPU`
9	to warm the cache hierarchy, then switch to `DerivO3CPU` (O3). The only
10	difference is who decides the warmup length:
11	
12	- Marker mode (m5op): warmup length = the instructions your guest code runs
13	  between the marker that switches in the warmup CPU and the marker that
14	  switches in O3. You decide it by where you place the m5ops. gem5 does not
15	  compute or default it.
16	- SimPoint mode: warmup length = the `warmup_interval` you pass (e.g.
17	  1,000,000 insts), placed right before each SimPoint. If fewer instructions
18	  exist before the SimPoint, it shrinks to all available. Default is 0 (no
19	  warmup unless you ask).
20	
21	## How the warmup works (same primitive for both modes)
22	
23	The warmup CPU is a `TimingSimpleCPU`: in-order, non-speculative, but it issues
24	real timed memory requests. So it fills the shared cache hierarchy (L1/L2/...)
25	with realistic contents. Caches are shared state (see model-switch spec 3.3) and
26	survive the CPU switch untouched. That is the whole point of warmup.
27	
28	What is NOT warmed: `TimingSimpleCPU` has no branch predictor configured in this
29	path, so O3's branch predictor, ROB, LSQ, and per-CPU TLB start COLD after the
30	switch. They are CPU-private state and are created fresh.
31	
32	```
33	fast model (KVM/Atomic)  --->  TimingSimpleCPU  --->  DerivO3CPU (O3)
34	   skip boot/init             warms CACHES           measure here
35	                              (predictor stays cold across this arrow)
36	                          ^                       ^
37	                     switch #1               switch #2
38	                                          (reset stats here)
39	```
40	
41	## Marker mode (m5op)
42	
43	m5ops raise exit events. Stdlib handlers: `src/python/gem5/simulate/exit_handler.py`.
44	
45	- `m5_work_begin` -> WORKBEGIN (hypercall 4), default = reset stats (:291-303)
46	- `m5_work_end`   -> WORKEND   (hypercall 5), default = dump stats  (:306-318)
47	- `m5_switch_cpu` -> SWITCHCPU, default = `processor.switch()`
48	  (`src/python/gem5/simulate/simulator.py:522`)
49	
50	By default, work_begin / work_end do NOT switch CPUs and do NOT warm up. You
51	build warmup yourself:
52	
53	1. Place a marker to switch Atomic/KVM -> Timing.
54	2. Run your code. That run IS the warmup (caches fill).
55	3. A second marker (often `m5_work_begin`) switches Timing -> O3 and resets
56	   stats.
57	
58	Warmup count = the dynamic instruction count of the code between those two
59	markers. It is in your hands, not a gem5 parameter.

# gem5 Warmup Before O3: Marker Mode vs SimPoint Mode

> Notes archive | Author: Nick Hung | Date: 2026-05-22
> Companion to gem5-cpu-model-switch.md (trigger source 3.6).

## TL;DR

There is no fixed warmup instruction count. Both modes run a `TimingSimpleCPU`
to warm the cache hierarchy, then switch to `DerivO3CPU` (O3). The only
difference is who decides the warmup length:

- Marker mode (m5op): warmup length = the instructions your guest code runs
  between the marker that switches in the warmup CPU and the marker that
  switches in O3. You decide it by where you place the m5ops. gem5 does not
  compute or default it.
- SimPoint mode: warmup length = the `warmup_interval` you pass (e.g.
  1,000,000 insts), placed right before each SimPoint. If fewer instructions
  exist before the SimPoint, it shrinks to all available. Default is 0 (no
  warmup unless you ask).

## How the warmup works (same primitive for both modes)

The warmup CPU is a `TimingSimpleCPU`: in-order, non-speculative, but it issues
real timed memory requests. So it fills the shared cache hierarchy (L1/L2/...)
with realistic contents. Caches are shared state (see model-switch spec 3.3) and
survive the CPU switch untouched. That is the whole point of warmup.

What is NOT warmed: `TimingSimpleCPU` has no branch predictor configured in this
path, so O3's branch predictor, ROB, LSQ, and per-CPU TLB start COLD after the
switch. They are CPU-private state and are created fresh.

```
fast model (KVM/Atomic)  --->  TimingSimpleCPU  --->  DerivO3CPU (O3)
   skip boot/init             warms CACHES           measure here
                              (predictor stays cold across this arrow)
                          ^                       ^
                     switch #1               switch #2
                                          (reset stats here)
```

## Marker mode (m5op)

m5ops raise exit events. Stdlib handlers: `src/python/gem5/simulate/exit_handler.py`.

- `m5_work_begin` -> WORKBEGIN (hypercall 4), default = reset stats (:291-303)
- `m5_work_end`   -> WORKEND   (hypercall 5), default = dump stats  (:306-318)
- `m5_switch_cpu` -> SWITCHCPU, default = `processor.switch()`
  (`src/python/gem5/simulate/simulator.py:522`)

By default, work_begin / work_end do NOT switch CPUs and do NOT warm up. You
build warmup yourself:

1. Place a marker to switch Atomic/KVM -> Timing.
2. Run your code. That run IS the warmup (caches fill).
3. A second marker (often `m5_work_begin`) switches Timing -> O3 and resets
   stats.

Warmup count = the dynamic instruction count of the code between those two
markers. It is in your hands, not a gem5 parameter.

## SimPoint mode

Warmup length math: `src/python/gem5/utils/simpoint.py:161-184`
(`set_warmup_intervals`):

```python
warmup_inst = start_inst - warmup_interval
if warmup_inst < 0:
    warmup_inst = start_inst        # not enough room: warm all available
else:
    warmup_inst = warmup_interval   # full requested warmup
self._simpoint_start_insts[index] = start_inst - warmup_inst  # back up the start
```

Restore flow:
`configs/example/gem5_library/checkpoints/simpoints-se-restore.py:138-167`

1. `schedule_max_insts(warmup_list[0])` -> run the warmup instructions.
2. At that MAX_INSTS exit: `dump(); reset()` stats, then
   `schedule_max_insts(simpoint_interval)`. To enter O3 instead of just
   resetting, call `processor.switch()` here. Same boundary, same count.
3. At the next MAX_INSTS exit: end of the measured interval.

Classic equivalent: `--standard-switch N` plus `--warmup-insts N`
(`configs/common/Simulation.py:631-632, 757-773`). `--warmup-insts` is the exact
warmup instruction count on the `TimingSimpleCPU` before switching to
`DerivO3CPU`. Default is None (off). Requires `--standard-switch` and `--caches`.

## Summary table

| Mode           | Warmup CPU      | Warmup count                              | Who sets it              | Default |
| -------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------- |
| Marker (m5op)  | TimingSimpleCPU | insts between the two markers             | you, via code placement  | none    |
| SimPoint       | TimingSimpleCPU | `warmup_interval` (capped at insts before the SimPoint) | `warmup_interval` param  | 0 (off) |

## Key caveat for both modes

Warmup warms CACHES only. O3's branch predictor and pipeline structures start
cold, so a too-short warmup gives optimistic-cache but cold-predictor results.
Pick a warmup length long enough to also fill the predictor history you care
about, even though gem5 will not do that part for you.

- `configs/example/gem5_library/checkpoints/simpoints-se-restore.py:138-167` -

Every demo under `tests/demos/` (T1..T7) should showcase its switching mechanism on
the SAME RVV-intrinsic GEMM, so the suite reads as "one workload, seven ways to
switch QEMU <-> vsim." Today demos split between `rt_c_v_regs` and `icount_spin`.

We reuse the existing GEMM `tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.c` (16x16x16 outer-product,
`__riscv_vle32` / `__riscv_vmacc_vx` / `__riscv_vse32`).

## Why two builds of one source

`qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c:471-485`: in icount/slice/bbv modes the default CSR
matcher is STILL registered. A workload containing `csrwi 0x7C0,0` drains AT the
marker and `exit(200)`s before any count target inside the kernel is reached. So:

- Marker-driven demos (csr, pc, archive, simpoint) need the markers -> MARKED build.
- Coun/profile demos (icount, bbv, slice) need a marker-free workload -> MARKERLESS.

Per user decision: one source, a preprocessor macro toggles the markers, built twice.

- `nm -n rt_c_v_matmul.elf` -> only `main`, `_hybrid_enter_pc`, `_hybrid_exit_pc`.
  The kernel is inlined at `-O1`, so a PC-range assertion has no symbol to anchor on.
  Fix: mark `vmatmul_kernel` `noinline` (also keeps it in the ROI per
  `runtime/rt_c_helpers.h:49-51`).
- Orchestrator CSR-drain is marker-driven: `tools/orchestrator/spawn.py:33` passes
  the plugin only `outfile=...`; `tools/orchestrator/checkpoint.py:237` sets replay
  `trigger_kind="csr"`. So T6 and T7 must use the MARKED build.

# Hybrid Simulator User Guide

Audience: a new engineer who wants to RUN the Andes hybrid simulator,
not study its internals. After this guide you can:

1. Build every artifact from a fresh clone.
2. Configure QEMU, vsim, and the orchestrator for a workload.
3. Pick a switching mode (M1..M8) and run one round-trip end-to-end
   with a concrete worked example.

For internals, read `docs/HYBRID_OVERVIEW.md`. For per-mode drill-down,
read `docs/switching_modes_tutorial.md`.

---

## 0. The one-paragraph mental model

QEMU runs the boring parts at MHz. vsim (Verilator + SystemC) runs the
small region-of-interest at cycle accuracy. They share RAM via an
`mmap` file. A magic trigger (CSR write, PC, or instruction count)
hands control between them. One run is three legs:

```
   QEMU1  -- state.bin + shared mmap -->  vsim  -- same files -->  QEMU2
   (fast)                                 (cycle accurate)         (fast)
```

The thing you choose per run is the TRIGGER that decides where each
leg drains and the next leg resumes. That choice is the "switching
mode".

---

## 0.5 Quick start with `./hsim`

`./hsim` is the canonical end-user entry point. It wraps the
developer-grade scripts documented in Sections 1-5 (`setup.sh`,
`tests/e2e.sh`, `scripts/run_e2e.sh`) behind four subcommands.

Four-command worked example - cold checkout to passing suite:

```sh
./hsim build                                            # qemu, vsim, plugin, simpoint, fixtures
./hsim list fixtures                                    # discover available fixtures
./hsim run tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf --mode csr     # one CSR-mode round-trip
./hsim test                                             # full e2e suite (defaults: MODE=both, JOBS=8)
```

Expected last line of `./hsim test`:

```
PASS 45, FAIL 0, SKIP 0 (elapsed: <Ns>)
```

Subcommand cheat sheet:

| Command                                                          | What it does                                                        |
|------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `./hsim list <fixtures|demos|modes>`                             | List available fixtures, demos, or trigger modes (M1..M8).          |
| `./hsim build [--what TARGET] [--dry-run]`                       | Build artifacts; targets: `all`, `qemu`, `vsim`, `plugin`, `simpoint`, `fixtures`. |
| `./hsim run <elf> --mode csr|pc|icount|slice [-v]`               | Run one ELF through the QEMU -> vsim -> QEMU round-trip.            |
| `./hsim test [--filter REGEX] [--mode csr|pc|both] [--jobs N]`   | Run the e2e suite; defaults `--mode both --jobs 8`.                 |

Run `./hsim <cmd> -h` for the full flag list of a subcommand. The rest
of this guide (Sections 1-7) documents the underlying scripts and is
useful when you need to bypass `./hsim` (custom env vars, single-leg
debugging, alternative CPU YAML, etc.).

---
